title: A bibliometric review of fishers’ knowledge research
content:
Abstract
Fishers’ knowledge is increasingly recognized as a valuable resource for fisheries management and a means of involving fishers in scientific and governance processes. Yet, despite rapid expansion—particularly in recent years—the full scope of fishers’ knowledge research has not been systematically reviewed. This study provides a comprehensive overview of the field by analysing its social, intellectual, and conceptual structures through bibliometric methods. Drawing on an analysis of 1223 documents, our findings reveal that while publications have grown exponentially, the thematic scope of the field may have reached a plateau. Fishers’ knowledge research has largely converged around studies of local ecological knowledge, often employing similar methodologies and using fishers’ knowledge to supplement or validate conventional scientific data. This trend seems to be driven by several cornerstone publications that anchor author networks. Nonetheless, other conceptual currents—particularly those emphasizing participatory approaches and knowledge co-production—are gaining traction and pointing to alternative directions in the field. Geographically, the literature is dominated by the Western Hemisphere, with Brazil and the United States as major contributors. Brazil stands out as a hub of productive authorship, collaboration, and thematic consistency, yet its global influence remains uncertain: its ethnographically distinctive terminology has gained limited international uptake, and citation metrics could not clarify its global impact. Yet this may also be understood as an outcome of enduring structural inequalities rooted in the coloniality of knowledge and epistemic injustices that shape the global production, circulation, and use of knowledge. Advances in the field are hampered by persistent challenges, including the limited visibility of African scholarship, inconsistent terminology, and a relative neglect regarding non-ecological aspects of fishers’ knowledge. By systematically mapping how knowledge is produced and accumulated, this review aims to prompt reflection, provide the basis to situate future research agendas and to complement other review techniques.
